questions.question: State the rule about commits and why it holds.

options.text: Only commit once certain that every other node will also commit
A node may commit independently and abort later if needed
Commits are revocable within a bounded window
Commits must be confirmed by a majority before becoming visible

questions.explanation: A participant may commit only after the protocol has established that every participant can commit. A later compensating transaction can reverse business effects, but it does not make the original atomic commit partly successful.

questions.question: Define two-phase commit?

options.text: An algorithm for atomic commit across multiple nodes
2PC is an isolation level exposed through SQL
2PC is a replication protocol exposed through the replication log
2PC is a locking protocol exposed through FOR UPDATE

questions.explanation: Two-phase commit makes a multi-node transaction all-or-nothing: every participant commits or every participant aborts. Databases use it internally, and applications can access heterogeneous versions through XA/JTA or WS-AtomicTransaction.

questions.question: What new component does 2PC introduce?

options.text: A coordinator, also called a transaction manager
A quorum of voters, always deployed as a separate cluster
A leader elected among the participants
A message broker between the participants

questions.explanation: Often a library in the application process, which turns out to matter a great deal for availability.

questions.question: Which nodes are participants in a two-phase-commit transaction?

options.text: Every node on which the transaction reads or writes
The coordinator commits on one node first, then propagates
The participants vote among themselves with no coordinator
The coordinator sends commit requests immediately and aborts later if needed

questions.explanation: Every node that reads or writes for the transaction is a participant. The coordinator first gathers durable prepare promises, then records and broadcasts one commit-or-abort decision.

questions.question: Which everyday ceremony is two-phase commit usually compared to?

options.text: The minister asking bride and groom individually
The minister marries the couple first and asks afterward
Each partner may retract consent at any time
The guests vote on whether the marriage proceeds

questions.explanation: Before voting yes, either participant can cause an abort. After that vote, a database participant has durably promised to obey the coordinator's final decision; unlike a person in the ceremony analogy, it cannot withdraw merely because it has waited too long.

questions.question: Give the first three steps of the detailed 2PC breakdown. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Obtain a globally unique transaction ID from the coordinator
Open participant-local transactions tagged with that transaction ID
Ask every participant to prepare; abort everywhere if any request fails
Have the participants elect a leader before the prepare phase begins

questions.explanation: The first phase establishes one transaction identity, performs participant-local work, and asks every participant to prepare. Any failure before all prepare votes are yes still permits a global abort.

optionExplanations.a: A globally unique transaction ID lets the coordinator and every participant associate retries, prepare records, and the final decision with one distributed transaction.
optionExplanations.b: Each participant performs its local reads and writes in a transaction linked to the global ID. This keeps local work provisional until the global outcome is known.
optionExplanations.c: Prepare asks every participant whether it can durably promise a future commit. If any request fails or votes no, the coordinator can still choose global abort.
optionExplanations.d: Two-phase commit uses a designated coordinator; participants do not elect a leader as part of each transaction. Adding election would not replace the prepare promises.

questions.question: Give the last three steps, including the commit point. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Each participant durably prepares, checks constraints, and votes yes or no
The coordinator records commit only if every participant votes yes
The coordinator retries its recorded decision until every participant applies it
If a prepared participant crashes, abort only the surviving participants

questions.explanation: The protocol has two crucial points of no return: when a participant votes 'yes' it promises that it will definitely be able to commit later, even though the coordinator may still choose to abort; and once the coordinator decides, that decision is irrevocable. Those promises ensure the atomicity of 2PC — single-node atomic commit lumps these two events into one, writing the commit record to the transaction log.

optionExplanations.a: A yes vote means the participant has durably recorded everything needed to commit later and has checked local constraints. It may no longer abort unilaterally after making that promise.
optionExplanations.b: Only unanimous yes votes permit the coordinator to durably record commit; any no vote leads to abort. Recording the decision is the coordinator's point of no return.
optionExplanations.c: After recording the decision, the coordinator can resend it until recovered participants acknowledge it. Retries are safe because every participant must apply the same irrevocable outcome.
optionExplanations.d: A prepared participant cannot be selectively abandoned or told to abort after global commit. Doing so only to survivors could make their result disagree with a recovering participant.

questions.question: Why can a prepared participant become stuck after the coordinator fails?

options.text: Because a participant that voted yes must wait to hear the outcome
Either the coordinator aborts or commits; the state is called pending
Either it fails before or after commit; the state is called blocked
There is only one case; the state is called prepared

questions.explanation: Before prepare, a participant can safely abort if the coordinator disappears. After voting yes, it has promised it can commit and cannot choose alone; until the coordinator's durable decision arrives, the transaction is in doubt.

questions.question: Why is aborting unilaterally unsafe after a coordinator crash?

options.text: That the coordinator decided to commit before crashing
Both databases received the commit request, so no ambiguity arises
Database 1 can safely abort after a timeout
Database 1 can safely commit after a timeout

questions.explanation: The only way 2PC can complete is by waiting for the coordinator to recover. This is why the coordinator must write its commit or abort decision to a transaction log on disk before sending commit or abort requests: when it recovers, it determines the status of all in-doubt transactions by reading its transaction log, and any transactions that don't have a commit record in the coordinator's log are aborted. Thus the commit point of 2PC comes down to a regular single-node atomic commit on the coordinator.

questions.question: Why is 2PC called a blocking atomic commit protocol?

options.text: Because it can become stuck waiting for the coordinator to recover
Because it holds locks; 3PC removes the locks and solves the problem
Because it requires unanimity; 3PC requires only a majority
Because it has two phases; 3PC adds a phase and is now standard

questions.explanation: Nonblocking atomic commit requires a perfect failure detector — a reliable mechanism for telling whether a node has crashed or not — and in a network with unbounded delay a timeout is not a reliable failure detector, since a request may time out due to a network problem even if no node has crashed. For this reason 2PC continues to be used, despite the known problem with coordinator failure.

questions.question: Quantify the performance cost of distributed transactions.

options.text: Over 10 times slower than single-node transactions in MySQL
About 10% slower, attributable mainly to the extra network latency
About twice as slow, attributable mainly to lock contention
Not measurably slower, since the extra cost is purely operational

questions.explanation: Many cloud services choose not to implement distributed transactions due to the operational problems they engender: they have a mixed reputation, on the one hand seen as providing an important safety guarantee that would be hard to achieve otherwise, and on the other criticized for causing operational problems, killing performance, and promising more than they can deliver.

questions.question: Distributed transactions are often lumped into one category. Which distinction actually matters?

options.text: Database-internal ones versus ones spanning heterogeneous technologies
Local ones versus remote ones, distinguished by network hop count
Read-only transactions versus read-write transactions
Single-partition transactions versus cross-partition ones

questions.explanation: Database-internal transactions do not have to be compatible with any other system, so they can use any protocol and apply optimizations specific to that particular technology — and can often work quite well. On the other hand, transactions spanning heterogeneous technologies are a lot more challenging.

questions.question: Explain how heterogeneous distributed transactions give exactly-once message processing?

options.text: Acknowledge the message only if the database transaction committed
It works by deduplicating messages at the application level
It works by making all message processing idempotent
It cannot be done at all without a shared transaction log

questions.explanation: The guarantee holds only for participants that speak the same commit protocol.

questions.question: What does XA standardize?

options.text: X/Open XA, for two-phase commit across heterogeneous technologies
eXtensible Atomic protocol, from 2001, supported only by Java EE containers
X/Open Atomic, from 1981, supported only by mainframe databases
eXactly-once Architecture, from 1999, supported by message brokers only

questions.explanation: XA standardizes two-phase commit across heterogeneous resource managers. Introduced in 1991, it is implemented by major relational databases and message brokers, allowing one coordinator to include both kinds of participant.

questions.question: Does XA prescribe how the transaction coordinator is implemented?

options.text: No; XA specifies the protocol API, not the coordinator's deployment
The coordinator runs as a replicated service, so an application crash is harmless
The coordinator runs inside the database, so it survives application crashes
The coordinator is stateless, so no recovery is needed

questions.explanation: The XA coordinator is commonly a library inside the application process, with its decision log on that host. If the process or machine dies, prepared participants remain locked in doubt until the same coordinator can recover its log and resend commit or abort.

questions.question: Why can't the rest of the system simply ignore an in-doubt transaction?

options.text: Locking — row-level exclusive locks are held until the outcome is known
Because in-doubt transactions consume memory on the participants
Because in-doubt transactions block replication to followers
They can be ignored, since in-doubt transactions are harmless

questions.explanation: If the coordinator has crashed and takes 20 minutes to start up again, those locks will be held for 20 minutes; and if the coordinator's log is entirely lost for some reason, those locks will be held forever, or at least until the situation is manually resolved by an administrator. While those locks are held no other transaction can modify those rows, and depending on the database other transactions may even be blocked from reading them — so large parts of your application can become unavailable until the in-doubt transaction is resolved.

questions.question: What are orphaned in-doubt transactions?

options.text: Transactions whose outcome the coordinator cannot decide
They are transactions with no participants; rebooting clears them
They are aborted transactions that were never cleaned up; a vacuum process removes them
They are duplicated transactions; deduplication resolves them

questions.explanation: Preserving the locks across restarts is required for correctness, which is exactly why rebooting cannot help.

questions.question: What is a heuristic decision in two-phase commit?

options.text: Heuristic decisions, letting a participant decide unilaterally
They are optimizations that speed up the common case
They are automatic retries with exponential backoff
They are coordinator elections after a crash

questions.explanation: A heuristic decision lets a participant escape an in-doubt transaction without the coordinator's recorded outcome. It may release resources, but risks committing where another participant aborted and therefore breaking atomicity.

questions.question: What is the 'key realization' about the coordinator, and what limitations follow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Treat the coordinator's decision log as a critical database
An unreplicated coordinator is a system-wide single point of failure
An embedded coordinator makes an otherwise stateless application server stateful
The coordinator must run inside every participant database for acceptable latency

questions.explanation: The coordinator is a database, a single point of failure, and a destroyer of statelessness.

optionExplanations.a: The coordinator's durable decision log is authoritative transaction state, so it needs database-grade backup and recovery. Treating it as disposable middleware can strand prepared participants.
optionExplanations.b: If an unreplicated coordinator and its log are lost, participants cannot learn whether to commit or abort. One coordinator failure can therefore block transactions across all participant systems.
optionExplanations.c: Embedding the decision log in an application process gives that process durable recovery state. This undermines the operational benefit of otherwise interchangeable stateless application servers.
optionExplanations.d: The coordinator need not execute inside each participant database; XA deliberately coordinates separate resource managers. Co-location is neither a correctness requirement nor a general latency cure.

questions.question: Why is XA limited to lowest-common-denominator behavior?

options.text: Because XA must be a lowest common denominator across data systems
XA is too fast for reliable logging, and it requires special hardware
XA cannot support more than two participants, and it requires synchronized clocks
XA requires Byzantine fault tolerance, and it forbids replication

questions.explanation: XA coordinates only operations that every participating product can express through the common protocol. It cannot solve product-specific deadlocks or isolation behavior, and one unavailable participant can prevent the entire commit.

questions.question: What must nodes agree on in a consensus decision?

options.text: Getting several nodes to agree on something
Formally, all nodes must propose the same value and the algorithm confirms it
Formally, the algorithm invents a new value not proposed by anyone
Formally, each node decides independently and they are later reconciled

questions.explanation: Consensus chooses one value from those proposed and makes every deciding node agree on it. Agreement and integrity prevent divergent or changing decisions, validity prevents fabricated values, and termination describes when a decision is eventually reached.

questions.question: Name and define the four properties a consensus algorithm must satisfy. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Uniform agreement: no two nodes decide differently
Integrity: no node decides twice
Validity: if a node decides value v, then v must have been proposed by a majority of nodes
Termination: every node that does not crash eventually decides some value

questions.explanation: Agreement prevents different decisions, integrity prevents a node from deciding twice, validity prevents fabricated values, and termination requires progress for nonfailed nodes. Safety covers the first three; termination is the liveness condition.

optionExplanations.a: Uniform agreement is the safety rule that no two nodes decide different values, including nodes that later crash. Without it the system would have split decisions rather than consensus.
optionExplanations.b: Integrity prevents a participant from changing its mind or deciding repeatedly. A decision is irrevocable, which lets later operations rely on it as stable shared state.
optionExplanations.c: Validity only requires a decided value to have been proposed by some participant, not by a majority. Majority support is an algorithmic technique, not part of the abstract validity property.
optionExplanations.d: Termination is the liveness condition that every noncrashed node eventually decides. It distinguishes a safe protocol that waits forever from one that actually makes progress under its assumptions.

questions.question: Which two safety properties form the core of consensus?

options.text: Agreement and integrity
Termination and validity are the core; agreement rules out trivial solutions
Validity is the core; agreement is an optimization
All four properties are equally core, with none more fundamental

questions.explanation: The uniform agreement and integrity properties define the core idea of consensus: everyone decides on the same outcome, and once you have decided, you cannot change your mind. The validity property exists mostly to rule out trivial solutions: for example, you could have an algorithm that always decides null, no matter what was proposed; this algorithm would satisfy the agreement and integrity properties, but not the validity property.

questions.question: What does termination formalize?

options.text: Fault tolerance — an algorithm must eventually reach a decision
Termination formalizes safety; 2PC satisfies it
Termination formalizes ordering; Paxos fails it
Termination formalizes durability; no algorithm fails it

questions.explanation: Termination is the liveness promise that functioning nodes eventually decide even when some nodes fail. Two-phase commit lacks it: after voting yes, a participant may wait forever if the coordinator never returns, even though 2PC preserves its safety promises.

questions.question: How many nodes must survive for consensus?

options.text: That a majority of nodes must be working for progress to be possible
At least one node, which is then able to decide alone
Every node must survive for any decision to be made
At least two-thirds of the nodes, in the non-Byzantine case

questions.explanation: Most implementations ensure that the safety properties — agreement, integrity and validity — are always met, even if a majority of nodes fail or there is a severe network problem: so a large-scale outage can stop the system from being able to process requests, but it cannot corrupt the consensus system by causing it to make invalid decisions.

questions.question: What fault model do most consensus algorithms assume?

options.text: That there are no Byzantine faults
They assume Byzantine faults, tolerating up to one-half faulty nodes
They assume no faults at all
They assume crash-stop faults with no bound

questions.explanation: Crash-fault consensus assumes nodes may stop or messages may disappear, but nodes do not deliberately lie or send contradictory statements. Tolerating Byzantine behavior needs more replicas and stronger protocols; the familiar threshold is fewer than one-third faulty nodes.

questions.question: Name the best-known fault-tolerant consensus algorithms?

options.text: Viewstamped Replication, Paxos, Raft and Zab
Only Paxos and Raft, which decide a single value each time
2PC and 3PC, which decide commit or abort
Gossip and anti-entropy, which decide replica state

questions.explanation: Viewstamped Replication, Paxos, Raft, and Zab replicate a sequence of decisions, usually as total order broadcast. Production systems should use well-tested implementations because subtle election and recovery bugs can violate safety.

questions.question: Map the four consensus properties onto the total order broadcast guarantees they produce. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Agreement: all nodes decide to deliver the same messages in the same order
Integrity: messages are not duplicated
Validity: messages are not corrupted and not fabricated out of thin air
Termination: every message is delivered within a bounded time after being sent

questions.explanation: Total order broadcast makes no timing promise. Termination corresponds to messages not being lost. A clean one-to-one mapping between consensus properties and broadcast guarantees.

optionExplanations.a: Consensus agreement yields identical delivery sequences at every node: each log position is the same decision everywhere. Different message order would imply different decisions.
optionExplanations.b: Consensus integrity makes each log-position decision irrevocable and nonrepeating, which corresponds to a message not being delivered twice at one node.
optionExplanations.c: Validity prevents the protocol from inventing or corrupting a proposed value. For broadcast, delivered messages must be messages that were actually sent.
optionExplanations.d: Termination promises eventual delivery under the model's progress assumptions, not a fixed time bound. Asynchronous networks can delay a correct delivery arbitrarily long.

questions.question: What distinguishes manual failover from consensus-based leader election?

options.text: A human chooses the replacement leader
Leader-based replication uses consensus implicitly via quorums
Automatic failover avoids consensus entirely
Manual failover satisfies termination

questions.explanation: Manual failover delegates the agreement decision to a human operator. That can preserve safety, but progress is limited by human response and is not the automatic termination guarantee supplied by a consensus protocol.

questions.question: What weaker guarantee do the protocols make about leaders?

options.text: They use epoch numbers, guaranteeing a unique leader per epoch
They guarantee a unique leader at all times; the number is the sequence number
They guarantee no leader; the number is the round number
The epoch number is called the zxid in all three

questions.explanation: Consensus protocols may temporarily have leaders from different epochs, but they guarantee one leader within an epoch and prefer the higher epoch. Paxos calls it a ballot, Viewstamped Replication a view, and Raft a term.

questions.question: How do epoch numbers advance?

options.text: An election with a monotonically increasing epoch number
Epoch numbers are assigned randomly, and the lower one prevails
Epoch numbers come from wall-clock time, and the later one prevails
Epoch numbers never change once assigned

questions.explanation: Each election advances a monotonically increasing epoch. If leaders from different epochs overlap, replicas accept the higher epoch and reject stale requests from the older leader.

questions.question: Why can't a node simply trust that it is the leader?

options.text: Because a node cannot trust its own judgment about being leader
Because a leader is elected purely by its timestamp
Because leadership is transferred on every single write
It can trust itself, since leadership is self-certifying

questions.explanation: Majority acceptance, not self-assertion, is what confers leadership.

questions.question: Walk the quorum-overlap argument?

options.text: Two rounds of voting: one for the leader, one for its proposal
The two quorums must be disjoint in order to avoid bias
Only a single round of voting is actually needed
Both of the quorums are required to be unanimous

questions.explanation: Consensus uses a majority to elect a leader and another majority to accept a proposal. Any two majorities overlap, so the proposal vote must encounter a node aware of a later election; if it does not, the current leader can safely proceed.

questions.question: How does epoch voting differ from two-phase commit? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In 2PC the coordinator is not elected
Fault-tolerant consensus algorithms only require votes from a majority of nodes, whereas 2PC requires a 'yes' vote from every participant
Consensus algorithms define a recovery process by which nodes can get into a consistent state after a new leader is elected, ensuring that the safety properties are always met
2PC relies on epoch numbers whereas consensus algorithms manage without them

questions.explanation: These differences are key to the correctness and fault tolerance of a consensus algorithm.

optionExplanations.a: In two-phase commit the coordinator is configured or chosen externally and is not made fault tolerant by the protocol itself. Consensus elects leaders through numbered terms or epochs.
optionExplanations.b: Consensus can decide with a quorum because intersecting majorities preserve prior decisions despite minority failure. Two-phase commit needs every participant's yes because each owns part of the transaction.
optionExplanations.c: After leader change, a consensus protocol reconciles logs so the new leader preserves every committed decision. Plain two-phase commit leaves prepared participants blocked if the coordinator is unavailable.
optionExplanations.d: Epoch numbers are a consensus mechanism for distinguishing successive leaders. Standard two-phase commit does not depend on elected epochs while consensus does.

questions.question: What safety result do consensus algorithms provide despite failures and uncertainty?

options.text: One irrevocable decision accepted by all nonfaulty participants
They provide eventual consistency with no majority requirement
They require only two nodes to tolerate one failure
They are fully asynchronous with no replication cost

questions.explanation: Consensus preserves agreement and irrevocability even when some nodes fail or messages are delayed. It does not guarantee low latency or progress during every network condition.

questions.question: Give the remaining limitations of consensus algorithms. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Static membership complicates adding or removing voting nodes
Variable delay causes false suspicions and disruptive leader elections
One unreliable link can cause pathological leadership churn
Any merely slow node is Byzantine and immediately violates safety

questions.explanation: Three further limitations: membership, timeouts and pathological link failures. Other consensus algorithms have been designed to be more robust to unreliable networks.

optionExplanations.a: Changing the voting membership safely is itself a coordinated transition because old and new quorums must overlap appropriately. Static configurations avoid that complexity but hinder elasticity.
optionExplanations.b: Timeouts cannot distinguish a failed leader from a delayed one, so variable latency can trigger unnecessary elections. Safety remains intact, but availability and throughput may collapse.
optionExplanations.c: A repeatedly unreliable link can make one node alternate between reachable and suspected, causing leadership churn. Some protocols need additional defenses against this pathological pattern.
optionExplanations.d: A slow node is a crash-suspicion problem, not automatically Byzantine. Consensus safety is designed to survive delay; Byzantine behavior means arbitrary or malicious protocol violations.

questions.question: How are ZooKeeper and etcd usually described?

options.text: Distributed key-value stores, or coordination and configuration services
They are described as message brokers; the question is about ordering
They are described as relational databases; the question is about SQL
They are described as caches; the question is about eviction

questions.explanation: You rarely need to use ZooKeeper directly, since it is actually not well suited as a general-purpose database — it's more likely that you will end up relying on it indirectly via some other project, for example HBase, Hadoop YARN, OpenStack Nova and Kafka all rely on ZooKeeper running in the background.

questions.question: What is ZooKeeper's data-size design point?

options.text: Small amounts of data that fit entirely in memory
They hold terabytes on disk, replicated by quorum writes
They hold data in memory only, with no durability
They hold arbitrary data, replicated asynchronously

questions.explanation: ZooKeeper and etcd keep only coordination-sized data in memory, with disk persistence for durability. They replicate each update to every node in one fault-tolerant total order, which keeps all replicas in the same state.

questions.question: Which primitive gives you a lock, and under what conditions does the guarantee hold?

options.text: An atomic compare-and-set, which lets only one node win
A read-write register, guaranteed only when the network is healthy
A timestamp comparison, guaranteed only with synchronized clocks
A quorum read, guaranteed only with strict quorums

questions.explanation: Linearizable compare-and-set allows only one contender to acquire a lock despite failures. The holder must keep its session or lease alive, and downstream resources should still check a monotonically increasing fencing token so a paused, expired holder cannot act later.

questions.question: What prevents an expired lock holder from writing after a new holder takes over?

options.text: A monotonically increasing fencing token
Tokens prevent replay attacks; ZooKeeper uses cryptographic nonces
Tokens identify clients; ZooKeeper uses session IDs
Tokens are not needed with leases

questions.explanation: Monotonic ordering of all operations is what makes zxid a valid fencing token.

questions.question: Describe the ZooKeeper session and failure detection mechanism.

options.text: Long-lived sessions kept alive by periodic heartbeats
Clients poll on every operation; there is no session concept
The server pings clients once per hour; locks are never released automatically
Sessions end immediately on any connection interruption

questions.explanation: Sessions survive transient interruption but not sustained heartbeat loss.

questions.question: What can a client do beyond reading another client's values?

options.text: Watching keys for changes, so clients learn when they change
It can only poll, since watches are not supported at all
It can subscribe, but only to keys that it created itself
It receives notifications only when its session ends

questions.explanation: Of ZooKeeper's four features, only the linearizable atomic operations really require consensus — however, it is the combination of these features that makes systems like ZooKeeper so useful for distributed coordination.

questions.question: Where does the ZooKeeper and Chubby model work well? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Electing a leader or primary and failing it over
Assigning resource partitions to nodes
Rebalancing partitions as cluster membership changes
Storing the application's large primary dataset directly

questions.explanation: These tasks can be achieved by judicious use of atomic operations, ephemeral nodes and notifications in ZooKeeper — and if done correctly, this approach allows the application to automatically recover from faults without human intervention. It's not easy, despite the appearance of libraries such as Apache Curator that provide higher-level tools on top of the ZooKeeper client API, but it is still much better than attempting to implement the necessary consensus algorithms from scratch, which has a poor success record.

optionExplanations.a: Ephemeral nodes, atomic creation, and watches let contenders agree on one current leader and notice its session failure. Applications avoid implementing election and failover consensus themselves.
optionExplanations.b: Coordination metadata can assign each resource partition to exactly one worker. Watches then notify workers when ownership changes so processing can follow the agreed assignment.
optionExplanations.c: Membership changes can trigger a coordinated reassignment recorded in ZooKeeper or Chubby. The service supplies the small, strongly consistent state needed to rebalance safely.
optionExplanations.d: Coordination services are optimized for small, slowly changing metadata, not high-volume application records. Using one as the primary data store would create a throughput and capacity bottleneck.

questions.question: An application grows to thousands of nodes. Why can't the coordination mechanism grow with it?

options.text: Because majority votes over that many nodes would be too inefficient
Because ZooKeeper has a hard limit of 100 nodes
Because clients cannot connect to more than three nodes
It can grow; ZooKeeper scales its voting set with the cluster

questions.explanation: A small fixed voting set serving many clients is the architectural answer.

questions.question: What kind of data belongs in ZooKeeper, and what doesn't?

options.text: Slow-changing data, such as which node is the current leader
High-frequency runtime state belongs in ZooKeeper; slow-changing metadata does not
Both kinds belong in ZooKeeper
ZooKeeper should hold application records because its replicated log is optimized for bulk data

questions.explanation: ZooKeeper is suited to slowly changing coordination metadata such as membership, leases, and partition ownership. High-volume application records belong in a database or object store designed for that workload.

questions.question: Does service discovery require consensus?

options.text: Service discovery
Yes, service discovery strictly requires linearizability
No, and neither does leader election
Yes, because IP addresses must be unique

questions.explanation: Although service discovery does not require consensus, leader election does — so if your consensus system already knows who the leader is, it can make sense to also use that information to help other services discover who the leader is. For this purpose some consensus systems support read-only caching replicas, which asynchronously receive the log of all decisions of the consensus algorithm but do not actively participate in voting, and are therefore able to serve read requests that do not need to be linearizable.

questions.question: What does a membership service decide?

options.text: Which nodes are currently active and live members of the cluster
A membership service detects failures perfectly using timeouts
A membership service avoids consensus by using gossip
A membership service requires synchronized clocks

questions.explanation: Agreement without accuracy is still valuable. Research into membership services goes back to the 1980s and has been important for building highly reliable systems, for example for air traffic control.

questions.question: Which problems are equivalent to consensus? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Linearizable compare-and-set registers, which must atomically decide whether to set their value based on whether the current value equals the parameter given in the operation; and atomic transaction commit, where a database must decide whether to commit or abort a distributed transaction
Total order broadcast, where the messaging system must decide on the order in which to deliver messages

Locks and leases, where when several clients are racing to grab a lock or lease the lock decides which one successfully acquired it; and membership/coordination service, where given a failure detector such as timeouts the system must decide which nodes are alive and which should be considered dead because their sessions timed out
Uniqueness constraint, where concurrent transactions creating the same key must all be rejected in order to keep the system safe

questions.explanation: One of them must be allowed to succeed — the constraint decides which, rather than rejecting them all. The remaining two equivalent problems are atomic transaction commit and membership/coordination services. Six problems, equivalent in the sense that if you have a solution for one of them, you can easily transform it into a solution for one of the others. Achieving consensus means deciding something in such a way that all nodes agree on what was decided, and such that the decision is irrevocable.

optionExplanations.a: Linearizable compare-and-set must choose one atomic outcome for a contested value, and atomic commit must choose one outcome for all participants. Either decision can be reduced to consensus.
optionExplanations.b: Total-order broadcast repeatedly decides the next message in one common sequence. A consensus primitive can build that sequence, and the sequence can in turn implement consensus.
optionExplanations.c: Lock acquisition chooses one winner among contenders, while membership services choose which nodes count as present. Both require an agreed, irrevocable shared decision.
optionExplanations.d: A uniqueness constraint normally allows exactly one concurrent claimant to succeed, not rejection of every claimant. The option removes the winner-selection problem and therefore misstates the equivalence.

questions.question: Under what conditions are all six problems straightforward?

options.text: They are straightforward on a single node, or with a single decider
When a majority of the nodes agree, with no leader needed
When clocks are synchronized to within a millisecond
When the underlying network is reliable enough

questions.explanation: Vesting decisions in one node makes them easy and makes that node a single point of failure.

questions.question: Give the three ways to handle leader failure and the objections. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Wait for the old leader, which may block forever
Use manual failover, which is slow human consensus
Elect a new leader automatically with a proven consensus protocol
Permit concurrent leaders and rely on conflict resolution for consensus

questions.explanation: Waiting preserves safety but may block forever; manual replacement depends on a human; automatic replacement needs consensus. Only the last option provides protocol-driven progress through leader failure.

optionExplanations.a: Waiting avoids two leaders and therefore preserves safety, but a permanently failed leader means the system may never resume. It sacrifices liveness rather than solving failover.
optionExplanations.b: An operator can gather evidence and designate a replacement, effectively performing slow consensus outside the protocol. Safety depends on human coordination and recovery time is unpredictable.
optionExplanations.c: A proven consensus protocol elects one replacement through quorum agreement and numbered epochs. This supplies automatic progress while fencing leaders from older epochs.
optionExplanations.d: Allowing concurrent leaders abandons the single agreed leadership decision. Conflict resolution may merge ordinary data later, but it cannot make both leaders' exclusive actions safe.

questions.question: A single-leader database provides linearizability without running consensus on every write. So why does it still require consensus?

options.text: Because it still needs consensus to elect a leader and handle failover
It does not require consensus at any point during its operation
It requires consensus on every write, contrary to the claim
It requires consensus for its reads but never for its writes

questions.explanation: Consensus relocated and made rare, not eliminated. In order to elect a leader, we first need a leader.

questions.question: What role do tools like ZooKeeper play for an application?

options.text: An 'outsourced' consensus, failure detection and membership service
As a general-purpose database that replaces relational systems
As a message broker for high-throughput streams
As a library you should reimplement yourself for your use case

questions.explanation: Hard to use, much better than the alternative of rolling your own.
